cases.name: room_create_rejects_an_out_of_bounds_name_with_room_name_invalid
cases.intent: Gives room.create the error case the corpus rule requires, using room.create's OWN code rather than the generic invalid_argument its two existing malformed cases already assert. Probes the two edges no plausible name bound can admit -- the empty string, and a name whose UTF-8 encoding is half of the served max_frame_bytes -- and asserts both are refused as room_name_invalid with no room and no genesis event authored. Catches (a) a daemon that enforces no name bound at all, so a client can write an unbounded string into a signed genesis event that every member must then store and render; (b) a daemon that collapses a name-bound refusal into invalid_argument, which a client cannot distinguish from a missing field and therefore cannot present as 'that name will not work, pick another'; (c) a daemon that silently coerces a bad name (trims, truncates, or substitutes a default) so the room's signed name differs from the one the user typed. The spec assigns this code but states no numeric bound and serves none in the limits object, so this case deliberately pins no number -- see notes.

cases.intent: Gives room.list its own code. With a subject present and a room known to exist, the accepted-room index is made unreadable and room.list must answer room_index_unreadable -- never ok with rooms: []. Catches the single most damaging failure mode this operation has: 'I cannot read your rooms' rendered as 'you have no rooms', which a user responds to by re-creating rooms they already own and by concluding their history is gone. It also catches conflation in the other direction -- answering subject_absent (the subject is present and this is not that precondition) or room_not_available (a local storage fault reported as a membership fact). The final step proves the refusal was a read failure and not data loss: with the fault cleared, the same room lists again unchanged.

steps.note: baseline: the index is readable and names the room

assert.note: UNMAPPED dialect assert count_where_eq: {"path": "out.rooms", "field": "room_id", "bag": "rid", "value": 1} — needs manual retranscription

steps.note: the accepted-room index is made unreadable at the storage layer -- an I/O error or a permission denial on read, NOT a truncation or a delete. Nothing is mutated: the bytes are intact and only the read path fails, which is exactly the state in which answering 'you have no rooms' is a lie.

assert.note: UNMAPPED dialect assert not_returned: {"shape": {"ok": true, "out": {"rooms": []}}, "why": "an empty success is indistinguishable from a subject that genuinely owns nothing"} — needs manual retranscription

UNMAPPED dialect assert not_returned: {"shape": {"ok": true}, "why": "a partial list is also refused: this operation reads from local evidence and has no partial answer"} — needs manual retranscription
UNMAPPED dialect assert absent_key: {"path": "err", "key": "hint"} — needs manual retranscription

steps.note: the room was never lost; the daemon simply could not read it, and said so

cases.name: room_members_refuses_rather_than_fabricating_an_unresolvable_standing
cases.intent: Gives room.members its own code and pins the spec's hardest membership rule: room.members is THE authoritative signed answer to who belongs and in what standing, so when the fold cannot resolve one member it must say membership_unresolved rather than serve a list. Catches the exact regression v2 removes by name -- v1's fabricated default role, which returned 'member' for a subject the fold could not resolve -- and catches the subtler variants: defaulting standing to active, silently dropping the unresolvable member so the list looks complete and shorter, or emitting a null role. Attribution a UI uses to decide how much to trust a person must not be invented, and a member list missing a member is a worse lie than an error. The contrast step is load-bearing: room.timeline over the SAME room still succeeds and reports that author as an explicit unresolved variant, so this case also catches an over-correction in which one unresolvable event makes the whole room unreadable.

steps.note: baseline: both members resolve

member B's standing is made unresolvable in the membership fold -- the signed event that would establish it is present but does not resolve (an unknown signer, or a reference the closure cannot follow). B is NOT removed and NOT made inactive: those are resolvable answers, and the point of this case is the state in which the daemon does not know. [harness orchestration: unresolvable_member_standing]

assert.note: UNMAPPED dialect assert not_returned: {"shape": {"ok": true}, "why": "there is no partially authoritative answer; a list served here would be presented to a user as signed truth"} — needs manual retranscription
UNMAPPED dialect assert no_fabricated_role: {"path": "out.members", "forbidden_default": "member"} — needs manual retranscription
UNMAPPED dialect assert no_fabricated_standing: {"path": "out.members", "forbidden_defaults": ["active", {"state": "active"}]} — needs manual retranscription
UNMAPPED dialect assert absent_key: {"path": "err", "key": "hint"} — needs manual retranscription

steps.note: deliberate contrast with the step above: timeline states an unresolved attribution per event and keeps serving history, while members -- the authoritative answer -- refuses. Two operations, two correct behaviours, neither of them a fabricated role.

assert.note: UNMAPPED dialect assert no_fabricated_role: {"path": "out.events", "forbidden_default": "member"} — needs manual retranscription

steps.note: [harness orchestration: unresolvable_member_standing]
the refusal changed no membership state

cases.name: removing_the_rooms_only_authority_is_authority_cannot_be_removed
cases.intent: Pins member.remove's own distinctive code: removing an authority is authority_cannot_be_removed, never member_unknown (the subject IS a member) and never insufficient_standing (the caller's standing is not the problem — the target's role is). Catches a daemon that lets the last authority be removed, orphaning the room.

cases.name: archive_of_a_room_the_caller_still_belongs_to_is_room_still_active
cases.intent: Pins room.archive's own distinctive code: archiving an active room is room_still_active, because the archive surface exists only for departed rooms and opening one with live capabilities would lie about what the member may still do. Catches a daemon that serves the archive to an active member, which is the room.archive side of the departed-room boundary #91 fixes.

cases.name: activate_reports_transport_unavailable_when_the_room_cannot_go_live
cases.intent: Pins room.activate's own distinctive code: a room that cannot be brought live is transport_unavailable carrying the room_id, never a fabricated live:true and never the membership refusal — the caller IS a member; the network is what failed. Catches a daemon that reports a live room while no transport exists, which is the fake-state failure the status vocabulary exists to prevent.

steps.note: no transport path exists for this room (engine cannot start a session)
the room still reads Closed, never a fabricated live state

authoring_notes: INDEPENDENCE. I read only docs/protocol-v2.md, docs/shared-file-size.md, docs/room-attention.md, docs/security-threat-model.md, docs/dioxus-architecture.md and the v1 corpus/harness conventions. I deliberately did NOT open crates/jeliya-core/src/engine.rs, so no v1 response shape could be transcribed. The only v1 shapes I saw are those in ui/src/lib/conformance/corpus.json, and every one of them is avoided on purpose: no `endpoint`/`endpoint_id` on activate (v1's room.open), no `room_unknown` (v2 uses `room_not_available` because the non-oracle property collapses two codes into one), no `identity_id`/`identity.create`, no `ticket` string, no `data_dir`/`pid`/`port`, no `hint`, no `available`/`providers` count, no nullable `role`/`status`/`last_event_ts`.

STEP VOCABULARY (extends the v1 harness; the manifest must adopt it). Step keys: `call`, `as` (actor id; default = the case's primary actor), `in` (params), `save` {bagKey: dotted path in `out`}, `save_out` (whole normalized `out`), `save_error` (whole normalized `err`), `expect` (exact normalized match of `out`), `expect_subset`, `expect_error` {code, fields (exact, err minus code), fields_subset}, `expect_identical_to` (bagKey; deep equality after normalization), `expect_absent` (key names that must not appear at any depth), `expect_no_null` (no JSON null anywhere in the frame), `expect_push` / `expect_no_push` {t, room, match, within_ms, as}, `assert` (array of named predicates), and `control` for non-op steps (`disconnect`, `reconnect`, `paired_timing`, `inject_conn_event`). Errors are compared flat: the v2 envelope shows `err` as `{code, ...typed fields}`.

TYPE TAGS. Reuses v1's `<hex64>`, `<room_id>`, `<ts>`, `<number>` and adds `<string>`, `<bool>`, `<array>`, `<op_id>`, and `<variant>`. `<variant>` asserts that a tagged-variant slot holds a non-empty string token WITHOUT pinning the token — used wherever the spec requires taggedness but never names the vocabulary (reachability state, link state, cursor state, role). The non-oracle pairs depend on `<room_id>` normalization: the two errors echo different ids, and they compare identical only because both normalize to the same tag. The harness must normalize whatever id format v2 chooses; I did not assume v1's `blake3:` prefix, and `{"$unknown_room_id": true}` asks the harness to mint a well-formed id that names no room rather than hardcoding a literal (a v1 literal is exactly what the old corpus did).

SERVED-LIMIT SUBSTITUTION. `{"$limit": "timeline_page_max"}` and `{"$limit_plus": ["timeline_page_max", 1]}` require the harness to read the value from the `hello` limits object at replay time. This is deliberate: it makes the corpus itself obey 'no client may compile the value in', the same rule the shared-file-size policy imposes, and it means the boundary cases stay correct if the daemon retunes the page bound.

PRECONDITIONS PUBLISH BAG KEYS. `requires` names are contracts on the harness. Actors: `authority`, `member_b`, `member_c`, `joiner`, `outsider`, `principal_1`/`principal_2` (two distinct authenticated session principals on ONE daemon and one subject). Bag keys published: `rid`, `rid_1..3`, `rid2`, `rid_inactive`, `rid_left`, `rid_removed`, `subject_a`/`subject_b`/`subject_c`/`subject_o`/`subject_joiner`, `device_b`, `removal_event_id`, `unresolvable_event_id`, `small_blob`. `$op_id_new` is a fresh op_id per use; `$op_id_fixed` is one value reused within a case (that is what makes the replay cases mean anything). `quiescent_room` means no other actor authors during the case, which is what makes `expect_identical_to` across two reads legitimate.

HARNESS CAPABILITIES BEYOND V1's. `network_observation` (zero bytes/zero dials attributable to the room during a step), `store_observation` (data-dir snapshot equal before and after — this is how 'zero durable mutation' is checked), `network_offline`, `reconnect`, `timing_instrumentation`, `harness_fault_injection`, `connection_generation_fault_injection`, `unreachable_member_device`, `linked_member_device`, `subscribed_*`. These are harness obligations, not upstream blocks; only U1 cases carry blocked_on_upstream.

CODES THE SPEC NAMES, USED AS WRITTEN: room_not_available, room_not_live, policy_refused, insufficient_standing, invalid_argument, resource_exhausted. CODES I HAD TO PROPOSE because the taxonomy is described as 40 codes but only eight are spelled out, and #161 forbids satisfying an operation's error requirement with a generic code: `subject_absent` (the single answer to the missing-subject precondition, spelled to match hello's `subject.state: absent`), `membership_ended` {room_id, state: left|removed, at} (the standing family: safe to return to a FORMER member, who already knows the room exists, so it is not an oracle), `sole_authority_cannot_leave` (kept distinct from policy_refused because #161 requires per-operation distinctiveness and policy_refused is already claimed by room.archive), `cursor_invalid` {reason: malformed|unknown|foreign_room}, `member_unknown` {subject_id}, `op_id_conflict` {op_id}. Every one of these needs ratifying in docs/protocol-v2.md or the manifest before the corpus freezes.

BIGGEST INTERPRETATION — WHAT room.archive RETURNS. The spec says it opens a left or removed room as a local read-only archive with zero network and zero durable mutation, but does not say whether (a) it RETURNS the archived history itself, or (b) it opens a read-only session after which room.timeline becomes legal for an ended room. I chose (a): room.archive takes the same cursor/limit shape and returns {room_id, name, standing{state,at,by,event_id}, events, cursor, capabilities: []}, and room.timeline stays member-only. Reading (b) would make room.archive redundant with room.timeline for reads and would make it stateful despite carrying no M marker. The discriminator is the step in `lifecycle_left_room_refuses_every_write_and_every_live_read` asserting room.timeline returns membership_ended for a left room: if the spec ratifies (b), that step and the archive success cases flip to room.timeline.

LIFECYCLE VS LIVENESS. I treat these as two orthogonal fields because room.deactivate is defined as stopping live participation WITHOUT changing membership: `standing.state` in {active, left, removed} (tokens taken from the spec's own prose 'a left or removed room' and #161's 'ACTIVE room') and a separate boolean `live`. `room_deactivate_stops_liveness_without_changing_membership` asserts exactly this split, so a daemon that collapses them into one enum fails. Member `standing.state` uses the same three tokens. If the manifest picks different tokens, only the tokens change; every assertion's shape survives.

THE ROLE TOKEN IS NOT ASSERTED LITERALLY. The spec removes the two-vocabulary naming (log `admin` vs wire `owner`) and says 'one name, both places' without saying WHICH name. Inventing one would be authoring the implementation, so `role_vocabulary_is_one_token_across_every_surface` asserts cross-surface identity (room.list's role equals room.members' role for the same subject) plus authority != member, which is precisely the property the spec states and is spelling-independent.

THE CAPABILITY VOCABULARY IS ALSO UNSPECIFIED. room.list must answer 'what may I do in each' and room.activate returns capabilities, but no token list exists. So capability cases assert behaviour, not tokens: `advertised_capabilities_match_enforcement_in_every_lifecycle_state` requires the harness to exercise each advertised capability (must succeed) and each omitted write (must refuse). RECOMMENDATION: the spec should enumerate the capability tokens, or this case degrades to a harness-defined probe list.

op_id REQUIRED VS ACCEPTED. The spec says every mutating operation 'accepts' an op_id but splits mutations into naturally-idempotent and op_id-deduplicated classes. I read that as: op_id is REQUIRED for the deduplicated class (an undeduplicable room.create makes the stated retry policy unenforceable) and OPTIONAL for the naturally idempotent class. `room_create_without_an_op_id_is_refused` and `room_activate_is_naturally_idempotent_and_needs_no_op_id` pin both halves. If the spec instead makes op_id optional everywhere, the first case must flip — it is the one to change, not the second.

NO SERVED BOUND EXISTS FOR ROOMS. The limits object bounds frames, bodies, inflight requests, connections, transfers and timeline pages, but nothing bounds a room NAME, the number of rooms per subject, or the number of members. I therefore could not author boundary cases for room.create at all, and room.timeline is the only operation in this domain with a real at-limit/one-past-limit pair. RECOMMENDATION: add `max_room_name_bytes` (and consider `max_members_per_room`) to the limits object, or the corpus can never prove where room.create's argument bounds are — only that a missing name is refused.

UNDECIDED, ASSERTED ANYWAY, FLAGGED HERE. (1) Does a naturally-idempotent room.deactivate succeed for a room the caller LEFT? I assert refusal with membership_ended, on the ground that a mutating operation must not be accepted against ended membership; idempotency is not a licence to accept writes. (2) Re-removing an already-removed member with a FRESH op_id: the reply shape is genuinely undecided, so `member_remove_repeated_with_a_fresh_op_id_authors_no_second_removal` asserts only the durable invariant (no second event, standing unchanged, exactly one member row) and deliberately does not pin the reply. Both need a spec sentence.

SHARED-CODE CAVEAT AGAINST #161's OWN CRITERION. room.activate, room.deactivate and room.members all take `membership_ended` as their most-specific error, so the per-operation error requirement is satisfied as 'most specific applicable' but not as 'unique to the operation'. The manifest must either state that explicitly as acceptable, or the spec must add per-operation codes. I flag it rather than invent three near-synonyms.

NON-ORACLE CHECK ORDER IS THE REAL CONTENT. The threat model requires the accepted-room index to be the FIRST guard, so the corpus pins ordering, not just codes: room.peers must answer room_not_available (never room_not_live) for a foreign live room, and member.remove must answer room_not_available (never insufficient_standing) for an outsider. Those two cases catch the failure that a naive implementation makes first — the liveness or standing check running before the membership check and thereby confirming existence. The timing half is a separate case because identical fields still leak through a membership lookup that is measurably slower than a miss; I specified a paired sample of 200 with Mann-Whitney U at alpha 0.01 and a 1 ms median-delta ceiling, which is a starting point the manifest should tune against real jitter.

POSITIONS ON COMMITTED HISTORY IS AN INFERENCE. The spec states monotonic per-room positions for PUSHES and an explicit cursor for room.timeline, but does not say history carries the same positions. `room_timeline_events_carry_the_same_position_space_as_pushes` asserts it does, because stream.resync's contract ('the client names the last position it holds') is unimplementable if the position a client holds from history is not in the same space as the one it holds from a push. If the spec disagrees, that case must be deleted and stream.resync needs its own alignment mechanism specified.

BLOCKED ON UPSTREAM. Two room.peers cases carry U1: `room_peers_reports_a_typed_reason_for_a_device_it_cannot_reach` (the 'why not when not' half of the operation needs ConnEvent's typed offline reason) and `room_peers_ignores_a_stale_generation_teardown` (needs the connection generation). Per the spec these FAIL, they do not skip. The rest of room.peers — a path per linked device, room_not_live, and the membership-before-liveness ordering — is producible at the pinned revision and is not marked blocked. U2 and U3 do not touch this domain.

WHAT I LEFT TO OTHER DOMAINS. stream.subscribe's non-oracle behaviour for an outsider (the push stream is explicitly in scope for the non-oracle rule) belongs to the streams corpus, but this domain proves the adjacent half: a removed member gets its removal push and nothing after it. invite.mint/redeem appear only as preconditions in the late-join and unredeemed-invite cases; their own success and error coverage is the invites domain's.
